title: AI: Unexplainable, Unpredictable, Uncontrollable
pitch: A computer scientist argues there may be hard limits: advanced AI cannot be fully explained, predicted or controlled, so we should be far more careful about building it.

chapters.g: Sets up the AI control problem and the question of whether safe superintelligence is even possible, and defines what 'safe' and 'governable' would mean.
Argues we cannot predict exactly what a smarter system will do, because predicting it would require being as smart as it.
Even if an AI could explain itself, the explanation might be too large or too complex for humans to understand.
Limits on proving that software, and especially self-modifying AI, is correct. Every verifier needs its own verifier.
Looks at whether AI systems and models can really be owned and kept under one party's control once they exist.
The book's central chapter: arguments, from computer science and other fields, that a superintelligence cannot be kept fully under human control.
A taxonomy of the ways AI could become dangerous: on purpose or by mistake, before or after deployment, from inside or outside.
A catalogue of real AI failures and what they suggest about how failures will grow with capability.
Should AI systems be treated as legal persons? The risks of giving rights to systems that could out compete us.
Could machines be conscious, and how could we tell? Yampolskiy discusses tests based on illusions.
A proposal for value alignment: give each person their own simulated world that fits their values, instead of forcing one set of values on everyone.
Argues humans are not general intelligences in the full sense, which matters for how we define and measure AGI.
Examines common forms of AI risk skepticism and replies to them.

ideas: There may be impossibility results for AI safety, like there are in mathematics and physics.
We cannot fully predict, explain or verify a system smarter than us.
Control and capability pull in opposite directions.
Because of this, the burden of proof should be on those who build advanced AI.

args.a: Superintelligence cannot be controlled, so it should not be built.
args.c: Many researchers accept partial limits but argue that partial control (monitoring, AI control, interpretability) can still lower risk a great deal.

args.a: Unexplainability is a deep, permanent limit.
args.c: Interpretability researchers like Chris Olah and Neel Nanda have made real progress reading the internal features of models.

questions: Is 'we cannot fully control it' the same as 'we cannot make it safe enough'?
Which of the 'un' properties worries you most, and why?
What do you think of the personal universes idea?

quiz.q: What is the book's central claim?
o: Advanced AI cannot be fully explained, predicted or controlled
quiz.w: The title lists the three limits Yampolskiy argues for.

o: Each person gets a simulated world matching their values
Every country builds its own AI
quiz.w: It is offered as a way to avoid having to agree on one set of values.

quiz.q: Why does Yampolskiy say verification is hard?
o: Every verifier would itself need verifying
quiz.w: This leads to an endless chain, especially for self-modifying systems.
